title: An aging country: its pyramid, its dependency ratio and its choices

plot.label: Population pyramid of Country Z: the bars are shortest at ages 0 to 4, widest at ages 50 to 59, and the groups 65 and over are large, with more women than men at ages 80 and over

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the shape of the population pyramid of Country Z.

rubric.point: Identifies the pyramid as constrictive (a base narrower than its middle).
accept: A narrow base and wide middle (constrictive)

parts.sample: Constrictive: its base is narrower than its middle.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe the age structure of Country Z shown in the pyramid.

rubric.point: Describes the structure using the data: few children, the largest cohorts in middle age, and a large share 65 and over.
accept: Shortest bars at 0 to 4; widest at 50 to 59; large groups over 65
Few children, many middle-aged and older people

parts.sample: The bars are shortest at ages 0 to 4 and widest at ages 50 to 59, and the groups aged 65 and over are large, with more women than men at 80 and over, so most of the people are middle-aged or older and few are children.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain one demographic reason for the narrow base of the pyramid.

rubric.point: Explains that fewer births (a TFR below replacement) make each new cohort smaller.
accept: Low fertility or a falling birth rate makes recent cohorts smaller
A TFR below replacement means each generation of children is smaller than its parents’

parts.sample: Because women in Country Z have fewer children than earlier generations did, with a TFR below replacement, each new cohort is smaller than the one before, so the youngest bars are the shortest.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how Country Z’s elderly dependency ratio is likely to change over the next 20 years.

rubric.point: States that it will rise and explains why: large cohorts move past 65 while small cohorts enter working age.
accept: It will rise because the large cohorts aged 45 to 64 will pass 65 while small cohorts enter working age

parts.sample: It will rise, because the large cohorts now aged 45 to 64 will pass 65 while the small cohorts now under 15 reach working age, so there will be more people 65 and over for every 100 people aged 15 to 64.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain one economic effect of this age structure on Country Z.

rubric.point: Explains an economic effect with its link: worker shortages, higher pension and health costs, or higher taxes on fewer workers.
accept: Fewer workers, so jobs go unfilled and firms use machines or hire workers from abroad
More retirees, so pensions and health care cost more and taxes rise
Slower growth because the workforce shrinks

parts.sample: With fewer young people entering the workforce, firms will struggle to fill jobs, so they may raise wages, use robots or hire workers from abroad, as firms in Japan have done.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain how one government policy could reduce the economic effect you described in part E.

rubric.point: Explains a policy and how it works: immigration of working-age people, a later retirement age, or pronatalist incentives, with the link.
accept: An immigration policy admitting working-age people, so the workforce grows now
Raising the retirement age, so people work and pay taxes longer
Pronatalist policy, so more children become workers later

parts.sample: An immigration policy that admits working-age people, such as nurses and builders, would add workers at once, so more jobs are filled and more people pay taxes that fund pensions.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which this national pyramid can show where older people live within Country Z.

rubric.point: States a degree and explains that the national data cannot show differences between places inside the country (subnational scale).
accept: To a small degree: it is national data, so it cannot show which provinces or cities are older
To a limited degree: subnational data are needed

parts.sample: To a small degree. The pyramid is one national picture, so it cannot show which provinces or cities have the most older people; rural provinces that young adults leave are often much older than the capital, and only data at the subnational scale would show that.
